paragraphs: Momentum adds a dependence on previous updates to gradient descent, and practitioners often observe faster neural network training as a result. This paper develops theoretical guarantees for that acceleration. It first revisits strongly convex quadratic problems and establishes an accelerated geometric convergence rate that applies beyond the eventual, asymptotic behavior covered by several earlier results.

The analysis then extends to two specific neural network settings: a one-layer wide ReLU network and a deep linear network. With appropriate parameter choices, Polyak’s momentum improves the dependence of the convergence rate on a condition number. For the ReLU setting this number comes from a Gram matrix; for the deep linear setting it comes from a data matrix.

In both cases, the improvement replaces dependence on the condition number with dependence on its square root inside the geometric decay rate. This gives a precise mathematical sense in which momentum speeds convergence for the studied models. The contribution supports the practical motivation for momentum while grounding the guarantee in particular network settings and suitable parameter choices.
icml-2021-a-modular-analysis-of-provable.tldr: The paper proves that suitably configured Polyak momentum accelerates convergence for quadratic problems, wide ReLU networks, and deep linear networks.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a single GAN training scheme that accommodates different amounts of labeled data. It introduces artificial labels that can also incorporate and align with human labels when those are available. The approach assumes that generators can more easily map nearby latent vectors to semantically similar outputs than map them across separate categories.

Generated examples and their artificial conditioning labels provide training data for a classifier. That classifier then assigns labels to real examples, supplying supervision without requiring every real example to be manually labeled. An exponential moving average of the classifier helps improve these assignments. Because predictions can still be wrong, especially early in training, a self-attention mechanism refines labels and uses real-example labeling only when classification confidence is high.

Experiments on CIFAR-10, STL-10, and SVHN show that both self-labeling and self-attention consistently improve generated sample quality. The scheme can even outperform class-conditional GANs in the reported evaluation. These findings suggest that inferred labels, together with mechanisms for handling unreliable predictions, can provide useful training structure across different labeling regimes.
icml-2021-a-unified-generative-adversari.tldr: A unified GAN scheme uses artificial labels, self-labeling, and confidence-aware self-attention to improve generation across labeling regimes.

paragraphs: The Weston-Watkins support vector machine extends binary SVM classification to problems with multiple classes. The paper is motivated by empirical evidence that this formulation performs well among multiclass SVM variants. Its focus is the computation needed to train the model, particularly a subproblem that existing solvers repeatedly address using an approximate iterative procedure.

The authors introduce a new way to express the dual optimization problem. This reparametrization makes it possible to solve the recurring subproblem exactly. The contribution therefore changes a component used throughout the overall training algorithm: each call to that component can obtain an exact subproblem solution rather than relying on successive approximations.

For linear Weston-Watkins SVMs, the resulting solver shows a substantial speed advantage over the state-of-the-art solver when many classes are present. Exact subproblem solutions also enable a proof that the overall solver converges at a geometric rate. The paper thus connects a targeted optimization improvement with both an observed training-speed benefit and a stronger convergence guarantee.
icml-2021-an-exact-solver-for-the-weston.tldr: An exact solver for a recurring Weston-Watkins SVM subproblem speeds linear multiclass training and enables a geometric convergence proof.

paragraphs: Multi-task learning trains related tasks jointly, while meta-learning also targets rapid adaptation to unseen tasks with few labels. This paper examines how closely these approaches are connected. Both aim to extract shared structure from training tasks, but their differing formulations can make them appear to require substantially different learning procedures.

The authors show that multi-task learning shares an optimization formulation with a class of gradient-based meta-learning algorithms. They further prove that, for over-parameterized neural networks with sufficient depth, the resulting predictive functions are close. In that setting, the two approaches therefore give similar predictions on the same unseen task, connecting joint training directly to adaptation behavior.

Experiments support the connection: properly implemented multi-task learning is competitive with state-of-the-art gradient-based meta-learning on few-shot image classification benchmarks. The proposed first-order method is also an order of magnitude faster on large datasets such as mini-ImageNet. These results identify an efficient alternative to the costly second-order, two-level optimization often used in gradient-based meta-learning, while retaining useful adaptation performance.
icml-2021-bridging-multi-task-learning-a.tldr: Under specified network conditions, multi-task learning closely matches a class of gradient-based meta-learning methods and offers efficient few-shot adaptation.

paragraphs: Variance stabilization transforms data whose variability changes across observations into data with more uniform variability. This can make later analysis easier. Many existing approaches derive a transformation for a chosen parametric distribution, creating a tradeoff: simple distributions may poorly describe real measurements, while more realistic distributions may resist an analytical solution.

ConvexVST replaces the search for an analytical formula with a convex optimization problem. The authors identify additional structure within that problem to improve computational efficiency. Their method is nonparametric, and they show that it can stabilize variance for any finite discrete distribution, as well as discretized versions of continuous distributions obtained from real data.

The bioimaging experiments assess both the transformed data and their usefulness downstream. ConvexVST outperforms peer algorithms in making variance more uniform and in its effect on subsequent analysis, including denoising. The findings connect a broader optimization-based formulation with practical benefits: stabilization can be evaluated by whether it improves the analysis that follows, as well as by how evenly it distributes variability.
icml-2021-convexvst-a-convex-optimizatio.tldr: ConvexVST uses convex optimization to stabilize variance nonparametrically and improves bioimaging results, including downstream denoising.

paragraphs: Selective labels arise when an outcome is observed after one decision but remains unavailable after another. A decision policy consequently affects both immediate utility and the evidence available for future learning. This paper studies that interaction online, explicitly balancing the cost of acquiring information against its potential value for later decisions.

When individual features are ignored, the authors prove that the optimal policy uses a threshold. That threshold becomes stricter as more labels accumulate, and the analysis characterizes how quickly this happens. When features take values in a finite domain, the optimal policy consists of several such homogeneous policies operating in parallel, extending the simpler result to feature-dependent decisions.

For an infinite feature domain, the authors extend the homogeneous policy using inputs supplied by a probabilistic classifier and bootstrapping. Experiments on synthetic and real data show consistently higher utility for the proposed policies. The finite-domain method needs no parameter tuning, while the general extension has lower parameter sensitivity. Optimality is established for the homogeneous and finite-domain settings; the broader extension is supported by empirical results.
icml-2021-decision-making-under-selectiv.tldr: The paper derives optimal finite-domain policies for selective labels and extends them to general feature spaces using classification and bootstrapping.

paragraphs: This paper frames generative learning as constructing a distributional path from a reference distribution to a target distribution. It uses a Schrödinger Bridge, with the interpolation defined through Kullback-Leibler divergence. At the population level, the path is described by a stochastic differential equation whose drift changes over time, directing the evolution of the distribution.

To turn that description into a learning algorithm, the authors estimate the drift using two neural components: a deep score estimator and a deep density ratio estimator. They insert those estimates into the Euler-Maruyama method, which supplies a discrete procedure for following the stochastic dynamics. This connects the distribution-level formulation to computation from samples.

Under mild smoothness assumptions on the target distribution, the authors prove consistency of both estimators and of the resulting generative approach. The learned distribution converges to the target under that theoretical framework. Experiments on multimodal synthetic and benchmark data support the analysis and show performance comparable with state-of-the-art GANs. Image interpolation and inpainting illustrate practical uses of the formulation.
icml-2021-deep-generative-learning-via-s.tldr: A Schrödinger Bridge generative model learns stochastic dynamics between distributions, with consistency guarantees under target-distribution smoothness assumptions.

paragraphs: Bias amplification concerns how a trained model can strengthen biases already present in its training data. This paper examines the measurement of that process as one part of the broader path from social structures through data and models to social effects. Its central concern is whether a metric distinguishes the phenomena it is intended to capture.

The authors identify shortcomings in an existing bias-amplification metric, including mixing different types of amplification and failing to account for differences in protected-attribute base rates. They propose Directional Bias Amplification, a decoupled metric designed to address these issues. Their analysis considers both its technical assumptions and the value judgments involved in deciding what amplification should mean.

The paper also offers guidance for measurement: it cautions against predicting sensitive attributes and recommends confidence intervals because fairness measurements fluctuate across training runs. It discusses limits on what the metric captures. The contribution is therefore a more carefully separated measurement framework, accompanied by attention to uncertainty and normative choices, rather than a claim that one number fully describes a system’s societal bias.
icml-2021-directional-bias-amplification.tldr: Directional Bias Amplification separates forms of bias amplification while examining base rates, measurement uncertainty, and the metric’s normative assumptions.

paragraphs: Attention maps describe dependencies among the input tokens processed by a transformer. This paper starts from the observation that learning these maps independently at each layer can sometimes miss precise patterns. It proposes a general mechanism that lets attention develop across layers, using information from earlier maps to help construct later ones.

The design combines two ideas. Residual connections carry attention information forward because maps at different depths share useful knowledge. Convolutional layers model how those maps should change because early and late attention operate at different levels of abstraction. Together, these components allow preceding layers to inform subsequent attention while also accommodating changes in the relationships being represented.

The authors report significant improvements over various state-of-the-art models across image classification, natural language understanding, and machine translation. These results support the usefulness of the evolving-attention mechanism across both vision and language tasks. The architectural contribution is to make the relationship between successive attention maps an explicit part of the model, with both continuity and transformation built into that relationship.
icml-2021-evolving-attention-with-residu.tldr: Residual connections and convolutions let transformer attention maps evolve across layers, improving performance on several vision and language tasks.

paragraphs: Learning-to-learn methods can tune an optimizer by differentiating an objective defined over its training trajectory. This paper studies the difficulties of that outer optimization through a simple setting: learning the step size for quadratic loss. Even here, the gradient used to tune the optimizer can become excessively large or small, and the learned choice may generalize poorly.

The authors establish guarantees for this setting and show that a naïve meta-objective suffers from exploding or vanishing meta-gradients. A redesigned objective can keep the meta-gradient polynomially bounded. However, calculating that gradient directly through backpropagation still produces numerical difficulties, distinguishing a mathematical bound on the gradient from the stability of the computation used to obtain it.

The analysis also characterizes when the meta-objective must be evaluated on a separate validation set to ensure generalization of the learned optimizer. Experiments verify the theoretical findings and reveal a similar phenomenon in more complex optimizers parameterized by neural networks. The results make objective design, numerical computation, and validation data central considerations when learning optimization parameters.
icml-2021-guarantees-for-tuning-the-step.tldr: Analysis of learned step sizes exposes meta-gradient instability and identifies when objective design and separate validation data are needed.

paragraphs: Sequential measurements can contain both dependence across time and a background that changes in an unknown way. Distinguishing these components is a statistical challenge: apparent temporal structure must be assessed while accounting for the moving background. This paper develops an estimator and associated hypothesis tests for inferring serial correlation in that setting.

The estimator uses least squares with a total variation constraint on the background. That constraint encourages a piecewise constant description, which can approximate a broad range of changing backgrounds. The tuning parameter is selected using the Ljung-Box test to manage the bias-variance tradeoff, connecting the amount of background flexibility to the inference procedure.

The authors establish a finite-sample upper bound on estimation error using variational inequalities. They also derive a lower error bound through Fano’s method and show that their estimator is near-optimal. Simulations and a psychology study demonstrate strong performance relative to state-of-the-art methods. Together, the bounds and experiments support treating unknown background variation explicitly when estimating dependence in sequential observations.
icml-2021-inferring-serial-correlation-w.tldr: A total-variation-constrained estimator infers serial correlation amid changing backgrounds, with near-optimal error guarantees and supporting experiments.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning uses previously collected data to evaluate or learn a policy. A central difficulty appears when those data come from a distribution different from the target policy’s distribution. Existing theory allows sample-efficient learning under strong representation conditions, but also identifies settings where errors grow exponentially with the problem horizon unless distribution shift is mild.

This paper investigates those concerns empirically using features from pre-trained neural networks. The motivation is that sufficiently informative representations might support stable learning despite a mismatch between the available data and the target policy. The experiments include representations trained on the very task being studied, giving this possibility a direct test.

Across the evaluated tasks, substantial error amplification persists even with those representations. Stable offline learning is observed only when distribution shift is extremely mild. The findings challenge the expectation that features useful for supervised learning will by themselves support reliable offline reinforcement learning under larger shifts. The authors interpret the evidence as pointing toward substantially stronger requirements for success beyond the low-shift regime.
icml-2021-instabilities-of-offline-rl-wi.tldr: Experiments find substantial offline RL error amplification with pre-trained neural features, with stability observed only under extremely mild distribution shift.

paragraphs: Imitation learning can be hindered when demonstrations contain expert mistakes. Treating every example as equally useful may mislead an agent or slow its learning. This paper studies that problem within generative adversarial imitation learning, where earlier approaches often relied on additional preference judgments or confidence scores supplied by an oracle.

The proposed method learns how to weight imperfect demonstrations without imposing extensive prior information. Its mathematical analysis shows that the weights can be determined exactly by combining the discriminator and the agent policy already present in the adversarial imitation framework. This ties the assessment of demonstration quality to components of the learning process, reducing reliance on separately collected judgments.

The theoretical analysis suggests that using estimated weights can allow the agent to learn a policy better than straightforward imitation of the demonstrations. Experiments in MuJoCo and Atari show that the proposed algorithm outperforms baseline methods when handling imperfect demonstrations. These findings support weighting as a way to extract useful behavior from flawed examples while avoiding the assumption that every expert action deserves equal influence.
icml-2021-learning-to-weight-imperfect-d.tldr: The method uses a GAIL discriminator and agent policy to weight imperfect demonstrations and improve imitation without extensive prior quality information.

paragraphs: Matrix completion seeks to recover a matrix from only some of its entries. This paper addresses non-uniform missingness, where entries can have very different chances of being observed. Such variation affects the empirical risk used for recovery, making the treatment of frequently and rarely observed entries a central part of the problem.

The authors construct weights by controlling an upper bound on a newly defined balancing error. These weights adjust the empirical risk for non-uniform observations without explicitly modeling the probabilities that individual entries are observed. They can be computed efficiently through convex optimization, giving the approach a practical mechanism for incorporating the missingness pattern into recovery.

The resulting estimator has stronger theoretical dependence on observation probabilities than existing work in asymptotically heterogeneous settings, where those probabilities can differ in order. The paper also supplies a new minimax lower bound for a class of heterogeneous settings and numerical evidence of effectiveness. Its contribution combines a weighting procedure with a more detailed account of recovery when observation frequencies vary substantially.
icml-2021-matrix-completion-with-model-f.tldr: Convexly computed weights adjust matrix completion for non-uniform missingness without explicitly modeling observation probabilities.

paragraphs: This paper studies recovering every community membership in a symmetric stochastic block model. The graph is generated from at least two equally sized communities, with connection probabilities determined by whether vertices belong to the same or different communities. The maximum-likelihood formulation is discrete and non-convex, which makes direct optimization a challenging starting point.

The authors tackle that formulation using projected power iterations. Their method needs an initial assignment satisfying a partial-recovery condition, and existing methods can supply such an initialization. In the logarithmic-degree regime, they prove that the iterations can recover the communities exactly at the information-theoretic limit, reaching the statistical threshold identified for the problem.

With a qualified initialization, the stated running time is O(n log² n / log log n), competitive with existing state-of-the-art methods. Numerical results support and complement the theoretical analysis. The result shows that direct non-convex optimization can combine strong recovery guarantees with efficient computation in this model, provided the algorithm starts from a sufficiently informative initial community assignment.
icml-2021-optimal-non-convex-exact-recov.tldr: With suitable initialization, projected power iterations achieve information-theoretically optimal exact community recovery in the studied stochastic block model.

paragraphs: This paper studies the number of environment samples needed to solve a discounted Markov decision process. It designs quantum algorithms to approximate an optimal policy, the optimal state-value function, and the optimal action-value function. These quantities respectively describe how to act, the value of states, and the value of taking particular actions.

The algorithms assume access to environment samples in quantum superposition. The authors justify this access model when an environment simulator exists, such as a video game or another program. Inspired by value iteration, the algorithms use that quantum access to improve sample complexity relative to the best possible classical dependence on key problem parameters.

The reported gains are quadratic in approximation accuracy, effective time horizon, and action-space size. For computing the optimal action-value function, a matching quantum lower bound establishes optimality of the proposed algorithm’s sample complexity. The results therefore identify both an advantage and a limit within the stated quantum sampling model. Their guarantees concern sample requirements under that access assumption.
icml-2021-quantum-algorithms-for-reinfor.tldr: With quantum-superposition access to environment samples, value-iteration-inspired algorithms achieve quadratic sample-complexity improvements in key MDP parameters.

paragraphs: An agent with partial observations can learn by imitating an expert that has access to more information. However, this information advantage creates a problem: an expert may recommend an action whose value depends on details the trainee cannot observe. Existing asymmetric imitation approaches can consequently encourage behavior that is suboptimal or unsafe for the trainee.

The paper derives an update that adapts the expert to this information mismatch. Applied iteratively, the update maximizes the expected reward of the trainee’s policy. The authors use it to build adaptive asymmetric DAgger, or A2D, a computationally efficient algorithm that trains the expert and trainee together rather than treating the expert’s behavior as fixed.

The authors show that the trainee can safely imitate the modified expert and that A2D outperforms learning from a fixed expert or through direct reinforcement learning. The central contribution is to make the teacher responsive to what the learner can perceive. This aligns the demonstration policy with the information available when the trainee must actually choose an action.
icml-2021-robust-asymmetric-learning-in-.tldr: A2D jointly adapts an informed expert and a partially observing trainee so the expert supplies behavior the trainee can safely imitate.

paragraphs: This paper addresses statistical inference built on Lasso estimates in high-dimensional linear models. Its emphasis is robustness when the data depart from the well-behaved error assumptions common in earlier work. The authors propose a residual randomization procedure designed to accommodate settings that include heavy-tailed covariates and errors.

Heavy tails make unusually large observations more relevant to the analysis. The procedure also can remain valid when errors are clustered, so the inferential setting need not always treat errors as independent across observations. The authors highlight clustered errors as practically important and comparatively neglected in previous work. These features broaden the types of data conditions considered by the method.

Extensive simulations illustrate the wider applicability suggested by the theory. The method outperforms state-of-the-art alternatives in challenging evaluated settings involving heavy-tailed covariates or small samples, while remaining competitive in standard, well-behaved settings. The contribution is therefore a more robust route to inference using Lasso estimates, supported by theory and empirical comparisons across both difficult and conventional data regimes.
icml-2021-robust-inference-for-high-dime.tldr: Residual randomization supports robust inference from high-dimensional Lasso estimates in settings including heavy tails and potentially clustered errors.

paragraphs: Data poisoning attacks interfere with learning through the training data. This paper investigates when stochastic approximation methods can withstand such attacks, focusing on finite-width, two-layer neural networks with ReLU activations. Its main result gives a robustness guarantee for stochastic gradient descent under a particular condition on the learning problem.

That condition is a notion of separability in the reproducing kernel Hilbert space associated with the corresponding infinite-width network. The analysis uses this infinite-width representation to establish a result about training finite-width networks. Separability is therefore a substantive assumption behind the guarantee, tying resistance to poisoning to the structure of the data in that induced space.

The width requirements have an unusual feature: robust generalization needs both a lower bound and a distribution-dependent upper bound on network width. The result does not simply prescribe making the model wider. Extensive empirical evaluations support the theoretical findings. Together, the analysis and experiments identify a role for controlling model width when seeking robustness to poisoned training data under the stated separability condition.
icml-2021-robust-learning-for-data-poiso.tldr: Under a specific separability assumption, SGD-trained two-layer ReLU networks resist data poisoning when width satisfies both lower and distribution-dependent upper bounds.

paragraphs: StarCraft II provides a demanding setting for deep reinforcement learning, but the computational expense and complexity of successful systems make further research difficult. This paper introduces StarCraft Commander, or SCC, with efficiency as a central objective. It addresses the full game through improvements involving both imitation learning and reinforcement learning.

The authors report top-level human performance using an order of magnitude less computation than the demanding precedent motivating the work. SCC defeats GrandMaster players in test matches and top professional players at a live event. These results demonstrate strong play in the reported encounters while linking that performance to a substantially reduced computational requirement.

The agent also shows robustness against varied human strategies and discovers strategies not seen in human play. The paper presents key insights and optimizations behind its efficient training. Its contribution combines competitive gameplay with a reduction in the resources needed to obtain it, addressing one of the main obstacles that the authors identify for research on complex real-time strategy environments.
icml-2021-scc-an-efficient-deep-reinforc.tldr: SCC achieves top human-level StarCraft II performance with an order of magnitude less computation and efficient imitation and reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: SG-PALM learns conditional dependency structure from high-dimensional data organized as tensors, or multidimensional arrays. The goal is to describe relationships among variables while accounting for other variables. The paper combines a graphical model with a training procedure designed to make this inference both physically interpretable and computationally scalable.

The physical interpretation comes from the Sylvester generative model. The authors state that this model is exact for observation processes that solve a Poisson-type partial differential equation. This connects the model to a specified class of physical processes. Computational scalability comes from proximal alternating linearized minimization, the optimization procedure used to fit the model.

The authors prove that SG-PALM converges geometrically to a global optimum of its objective. They also demonstrate its scalability and accuracy on forecasting solar flares across space and time using multimodal imaging data. The contribution brings together a physically grounded model, an efficient fitting method, and a global convergence result, with a demanding forecasting application illustrating how those components work together.
icml-2021-sg-palm-a-fast-physically-inte.tldr: SG-PALM learns tensor dependencies with a physically interpretable model and an optimizer proven to converge geometrically to a global optimum.

paragraphs: A sketch preserves selected information about a visual concept, making drawing a possible source of supervision for learning image representations. SketchEmbedNet explores this idea by training a model to produce sketches from images. The paper focuses on what the model learns internally through that task and whether those representations remain useful beyond familiar examples.

The resulting model is generative and class-agnostic. The authors examine its image embeddings, which represent images in a form usable for further learning. They show that these embeddings carry useful information in few-shot settings involving new examples, new classes, and even new datasets. This tests transfer beyond the limited sets of object classes emphasized in earlier sketch-generation work.

The learned representations also display structure and compositionality, suggesting that the drawing task captures relationships within visual concepts. The stated contribution is the usefulness of sketch-producing training for representation learning. Its findings broaden the role of drawing models beyond generation quality and retrieval by showing that imitating sketches can yield transferable information for learning unfamiliar visual concepts from few examples.
icml-2021-sketchembednet-learning-novel-.tldr: Training a class-agnostic model to sketch images produces informative representations that transfer to new examples, classes, and datasets in few-shot settings.

paragraphs: An optimization algorithm can influence which solution a neural network approaches, even without explicitly adding a preference to the training objective. This implicit bias offers a way to study generalization. The paper examines adaptive optimizers on homogeneous neural networks, focusing on the direction approached by their parameters when minimizing logistic loss.

The authors prove that Adam and RMSProp approach the same parameter direction as gradient descent in the studied setting. AdaGrad behaves differently: its limiting direction depends on the adaptive conditioner that adjusts its updates. This distinguishes algorithms that might otherwise be grouped together simply because they all adapt their optimization steps.

To establish these results, the paper develops a unified framework using adaptive gradient flow and a surrogate margin. The findings provide a theoretical explanation for the generalization advantage attributed to the exponential moving average strategy used by Adam and RMSProp. The specific object of analysis is parameter direction for homogeneous networks under logistic loss, making the result a structured account of optimizer bias within that setting.
icml-2021-the-implicit-bias-for-adaptive.tldr: For homogeneous networks trained with logistic loss, Adam and RMSProp share gradient descent’s limiting parameter direction, while AdaGrad’s depends on its conditioner.

paragraphs: Laplacian representations describe reinforcement-learning states using eigenvectors of the state-transition graph’s Laplacian matrix. These embeddings capture the geometry of the state space and can support option discovery and reward shaping. For large or continuous spaces, learning an approximation is useful because the desired representation must be obtained without directly handling every state.

The paper identifies an ambiguity in an existing spectral graph-drawing objective: it has infinitely many global minimizers besides the intended eigenvectors. Consequently, optimizing that objective can produce a representation different from the target. The authors generalize the graph-drawing formulation and derive a new objective for which they prove that the eigenvectors form the unique global minimizer.

Experiments in gridworld and continuous-control environments validate the improved approximation of the target representation. The learned embeddings also produce more exploratory options and better reward shaping. The contribution links an objective-level guarantee to downstream usefulness: making the intended representation uniquely optimal addresses a source of ambiguity in training and improves the representations used by the evaluated reinforcement-learning methods.
icml-2021-towards-better-laplacian-repre.tldr: A generalized graph-drawing objective uniquely targets Laplacian eigenvectors and yields representations that improve exploration and reward shaping in experiments.

paragraphs: UniSpeech combines labeled and unlabeled speech during pre-training to learn representations that transfer across languages and domains. Its multi-task setup joins supervised phonetic CTC learning with contrastive self-supervised learning that is aware of phonetic information. The aim is to make the learned representation more closely reflect the structure of speech sounds.

The authors evaluate cross-language transfer on the public CommonVoice corpus. They report maximum relative phone-error-rate reductions of 13.4% against self-supervised pre-training and 26.9% against supervised transfer learning, with the comparisons averaged across testing languages. These results support combining the two learning signals as a way to improve speech recognition beyond either comparison approach.

A separate speech-recognition task tests transfer under domain shift and shows a 6% relative reduction in word error rate against the previous approach. Together, the evaluations connect the phonetic emphasis of pre-training with improved transfer in two settings. The reported gains concern recognition errors, providing evidence that the unified representation helps downstream speech tasks as well as capturing phonetic structure.
icml-2021-unispeech-unified-speech-repre.tldr: UniSpeech combines supervised phonetic and self-supervised learning to improve speech representation transfer across languages and domains.
